title: The hoona approach and the 7 vitality axes
description: The body knows how to regulate itself in the right conditions. hoona's 7 vitality axes: nutrition, sleep, movement, detox, nervous system, emotions, meaning.
text: We inspire, inform and support vitality in everyday life. There is no guru and no magic recipe, only a return to the fundamentals. A simple premise Our body is a living system with a natural ability to regulate itself. It has everything it needs to stay in balance, as soon as it is given the right conditions. In today’s world, this complex and wonderful system is put to the test. Amid the noise of constant and often contradictory information, we have lost sight of the basics: how to support our vitality, simply. The evidence of common sense means going back to the foundations, simplifying what has been made needlessly complicated, and finding the clarity to make everyday choices that support your balance. “We are often more attentive to the slightest warning light on our car than to our own body. Spotting the first signs of imbalance lets us act before the glass overflows.” Our role is to help you notice these signals, these “whispers of the body”, so that you can then make informed choices that suit you, with full awareness. The 7 vitality axes Everything is connected. Our approach is built around seven pillars that work like communicating vessels: acting on one supports your whole vital energy. And when one overflows, the others feel it too. Nutrition Food and hydration are our main sources of energy. We offer practical advice, tailored to your needs, for fresh, seasonal and anti-inflammatory eating, without going to extremes. We pay particular attention to the microbiota…

title: A longer exhale, the shortest path to calm
description: An out-breath longer than the in-breath sends the nervous system a signal of safety. No equipment, no special place.
headings: A longer exhale, the shortest path to calm
The exercise: 4 counts in, 6 counts out
Stress does not only live in your head
Taking care of yourself when everyone counts on you
Walking with poles in the Sonian Forest
text: An out-breath longer than the in-breath sends the nervous system a signal of safety. No equipment, no special place. Five rounds are enough to feel the difference. A longer exhale is one of the simplest ways to tell your body it is safe. When the breath going out lasts longer than the breath coming in, the nervous system receives a calming signal. No equipment, no special place: a chair, a bench or your bed will do. Why it works Our autonomic nervous system has two main modes. The action mode, which speeds up the heart and mobilises energy to cope. And the recovery mode, which digests, repairs and lets the pressure drop. Both are useful. What wears us down is staying stuck in the first one: full days, notifications, lists that grow longer at the end of the year. Breathing is the only automatic function we have a direct hold on. On the in-breath, the heart speeds up a little. On the out-breath, it slows down, under the influence of the vagus nerve, the long nerve that links the brain to the heart, the lungs and the belly. Lengthening the exhale gives this natural brake more time. The body gets the message before the head does. The exercise: 4 counts in, 6 counts out Settle in, back supported, feet on the floor. Breathe in through the nose for a count of 4. Breathe out slowly, through the nose or through barely parted lips, for a count of 6. Repeat five times. No more, to begin with. If 6 feels long, start with 4 and 5. If you feel light-headed, you are forcing it: go back to…

text: Before cleanses and green juices, a sort-out of the plate, the bathroom and the supplement cupboard. Then one simple gesture to support the liver, a hot-water bottle for thirty minutes. The word "detox" is everywhere, often sold in a bottle. At hoona, we start from a slightly less glamorous fact: the body already has everything it needs to eliminate. Liver, kidneys, intestines, skin, lungs, the elimination organs do this work day and night. The question is not how to replace them, but how to stop overloading them, and then how to lend them a hand. The first detox is to stop intoxicating yourself. Sorting things out, in three places The plate. Ultra-processed products, refined sugar, oils heated to high temperatures, alcohol every day: these are the liver’s main suppliers of work. More whole foods, in season, simply cooked, and the liver can already breathe. The bathroom. What the skin absorbs also passes through the liver. A shorter ingredient list on the shampoo, the cream and the deodorant is one load less. The supplement cupboard. Piled up for no reason, supplements become an overload themselves. Better a few, well chosen, than many, at random. That is a subject for a consultation, not for a shop shelf. The liver, the quiet organ It filters, transforms, makes the bile that digests fats, stores and distributes energy. When it is congested, you rarely feel it where it sits, under the ribs on the right. You feel it instead in heavy digestion, in tiredness that settles in, in…

title: Letting the body shake
description: After a fright, animals shake, then move on. We hold it in. The TRE method wakes up this reflex to discharge the tension that stress has left in the body.
headings: The psoas, the muscle of alertness
Taking care of yourself when everyone counts on you
A longer exhale, the shortest path to calm
text: After a fright, animals shake, then move on. We hold it in. The TRE method wakes up this reflex to discharge the tension that stress has left in the body. Watch an animal after a fright: it shakes from head to tail for a few seconds, then gets on with its life. That shaking is not leftover fear. It is how the nervous system discharges the adrenaline and cortisol mobilised to flee or fight. We have the same reflex. But we have learnt to hold it in: nobody shakes in a meeting, or in front of their children. The tension then stays stored in the muscles, and settles there. The psoas, the muscle of alertness At the heart of this mechanism, a deep muscle links the lower back to the thighs through the belly: the psoas. It is the first to contract in the face of danger, to protect the organs. In many of us, it never quite lets go anymore. A tight lower back, stiff hips, short breath, light sleep: so many signs that the body still believes it is on alert. We are often more attentive to the smallest warning light on our car than to our own body. Spotting the first signs of imbalance lets us act before the vase overflows. What the TRE method does Tension and Trauma Releasing Exercises, developed by David Berceli, is based on seven simple exercises. They gently tire the legs and the psoas, until the body itself triggers neurogenic tremors, those involuntary vibrations that start in the thighs and sometimes rise to the shoulders. Nothing to do, nothing to think: you lie down, let it…

title: The microbiome, the quiet foundation of vitality
description: Chewing, eating sitting down, choosing whole foods, drinking light water. Before any supplement, the microbiome feeds on simple gestures.
headings: The microbiome, the quiet foundation of vitality
Twelve habits that protect the microbiome
The first detox is to stop intoxicating yourself
Taking care of yourself when everyone counts on you
text: Chewing, eating sitting down, choosing whole foods, drinking light water. Before any supplement, the microbiome feeds on simple gestures. Twelve habits that protect it. Billions of bacteria live in our gut. They digest what we cannot digest ourselves, make vitamins, train our natural defences and talk to the brain all day long. At hoona, nutrition is the first of the 7 vitality axes, and the microbiome is its foundation: when it is doing well, energy, mood and immunity follow. When it suffers, you feel it in the belly first, then everywhere else. Good news: it feeds on simple gestures, long before supplements. It starts in the mouth The mouth is the first stage of the digestive system, and it already hosts more than 700 species of bacteria. Chewing slowly, putting the cutlery down between two mouthfuls, means handing the stomach a job already half done. Eating standing up, in a hurry, in ten minutes, is the opposite. A calm moment around the meal, even a short one, changes digestion. And a healthy mouth also means a gut less exposed to unwanted bacteria. Twelve habits that protect the microbiome Savour each mouthful, chew slowly. Eat sitting down, in a relaxed moment, with attention. Prepare your own meals: simple, quick, delicious, nourishing. Choose seasonal, local food, organic whenever possible. Cook in stainless steel, wood or cast iron, with gentle steaming rather than high heat. Prefer wholegrain flours and sourdough bread made from spelt, einkorn or buckwheat to…

title: Sleep begins in the morning
description: Clocks going back, screens late at night, broken nights. Before looking for a remedy, let's lay the foundations. The first one is morning light.
headings: The phone goes to bed before you do
Taking care of yourself when everyone counts on you
A longer exhale, the shortest path to calm
Walking with poles in the Sonian Forest
text: Clocks going back, screens late at night, broken nights. Before looking for a remedy, let's lay the foundations. The first one is morning light. Feeling slightly out of sync since the clocks went back? That is normal, and it is temporary. Your body runs on a 24-hour rhythm, and it has one favourite cue to set the time: morning light. As soon as daylight reaches your eyes, your body knows the day has begun. It switches on its daytime rhythm and, quietly, starts preparing the coming night. The sleep cycle starts... in the morning. Before any remedy, the basics Before deciding there is a sleep problem, we invite you to check that the basic conditions are in place. It is less spectacular than a supplement or a gadget, and it is what changes the most. The bedroom. Cool, between 17 and 19 °C. Dark, as close to complete darkness as possible: a blackout blind often settles the matter. Quiet, by tracking down the stray noises that can be removed. And no phone switched on. The schedule. Regularity above all: going to bed and getting up at similar times, weekdays and weekends. The body likes trains that run on time. The plate. A light evening meal, eaten early, two hours at the latest before bed. Tea and coffee remain stimulants: we keep them for the morning. Movement. Moving enough during the day to build real physical tiredness, preferably outdoors. Intense sport in the evening, on the other hand, wakes you up. title: Walking with poles in the Sonian Forest

text: Nordic walking works up to 90 % of the muscles without loading the knees, and the forest lowers cortisol. What it brings, how to start, how long to walk. Movement is one of the 7 hoona vitality axes, and the simplest one to set in motion. No gym, no membership: a pair of poles, good shoes and a path. In Tervuren, the path starts at the door of the centre and enters the Sonian Forest. What Nordic walking does for the body Done well, it engages 80 to 90 % of the muscle mass. Energy expenditure is 30 to 40 % higher than ordinary walking, with a release of endorphins but without the rise in cortisol that often comes with jogging. The poles spread the body’s weight over four points instead of two: ankles and knees are spared. With the technique, the deep muscles of the back grow stronger. The twisting movements massage the organs of the belly and give them more room. Opening the rib cage improves breathing; the dynamic stretches along the whole muscular chain support lymphatic drainage. What the forest does for the nervous system Walking under the trees is not just about scenery. The calm their presence brings can be measured: the heart rate slows, cortisol, adrenaline and blood pressure drop, the nervous system finds its balance. Daylight sets the internal clock and supports vitamin D. And since it is hard to walk with poles while your mind is elsewhere, the practice brings you back into the body, the posture, the breath. title: Taking care of yourself when everyone counts on you
description: You are the person others lean on, and you come last. Changing that order is not selfish. It is the condition for carrying on.
headings: Taking care of yourself when everyone counts on you
The trap of those who hold everything together
And when the fatigue has settled in
A longer exhale, the shortest path to calm
Walking with poles in the Sonian Forest
text: You are the person others lean on, and you come last. Changing that order is not selfish. It is the condition for carrying on. There is a question we hear almost every week at the centre, phrased a thousand ways: "How do I take care of myself when everyone counts on me?" It comes from people who hold a lot. A family, a team, ageing parents, friends who call when things go wrong. Reliable, active people, the ones you can count on. And who, over time, forget themselves. The trap of those who hold everything together This profile has a strength: it keeps moving. It solves, anticipates, organises, and finds in being useful a real source of meaning. It also has a blind spot: its ability to keep going masks how empty it is. Nobody sees it stop, so nobody worries. Neither does the person. The signs come through the body before they come through the mind. Nights get shorter. Patience wears thin. Thoughts loop in the evening. Listening to someone, even someone you love, takes effort. And the usual answer is to push a little harder: manage more, run more, sleep less. It keeps the illusion of control, for a while. We are often more attentive to the smallest warning light on our car than to our own body. It is not selfish Many people in this situation have absorbed a simple rule: others first. Taking time for themselves then feels like a fault, or a luxury for later, when everything is calm. Everything is never calm. We suggest another reading. Taking care of yourself is not a bracket…
